title: Trump: Barr's DOJ drops criminal case against Michael Flynn
description_short: Trump: Barr's DOJ drops criminal case against Michael Flynn
description_medium: On May 7, 2020, the Justice Department moved to drop its criminal case against Michael Flynn, a former national security adviser who had pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about his Russia contacts. Attorney General William Barr had appointed an outside prosecutor to review the case, and Flynn’s lawyers cited newly disclosed material. The move drew criticism from former prosecutors and lawmakers as an unusual reversal after a guilty plea.
description_long:
The Justice Department moved on May 7, 2020, to dismiss the criminal case against Michael Flynn, Donald Trump’s former national security adviser. Flynn had pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about his contacts with Russia. Attorney General William Barr assigned an outside prosecutor to review the case, and Flynn’s lawyers relied on documents they said showed prosecutorial misconduct. The department’s decision followed that review and became a major controversy over political influence in federal law enforcement.

Former prosecutors questioned the move, and House Judiciary Committee chairman Jerrold Nadler called it a politicized decision to let a presidential ally walk away from a guilty plea. The judge did not immediately dismiss the case, and the dispute continued after the Justice Department’s filing. Trump later pardoned Flynn in November 2020. The May entry records the department’s effort to end the prosecution and the public dispute about Barr’s role; it does not say Flynn’s original plea was erased immediately on May 7. The decision was one of the most visible examples of Barr’s intervention in cases arising from the Russia investigation and raised concerns about whether ordinary charging decisions were being applied consistently.

title: Trump: DOJ & DHS dismantle election security and foreign-sabotage safeguards
description_short: Trump: DOJ & DHS dismantle election security and foreign-sabotage safeguards
description_medium: On February 20, 2025, the Trump administration reassigned dozens of officials working on foreign election interference at the FBI and forced out others at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The teams had tracked influence operations and worked on safeguards against cyberattacks on voting systems. The changes drew warnings from security experts and election officials that the United States would be less prepared to counter covert foreign activity.
description_long:
The Trump administration dismantled or reassigned parts of the federal election-security response on February 20, 2025. Reporting cited in the timeline said several dozen officials working on foreign influence at the FBI were reassigned, while others at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency were forced out. Their work included monitoring false online content and protecting election systems from cyberattacks or other disruption. During the 2024 election, these teams had tracked influence activity attributed to Russia, China, and Iran.

The changes alarmed election-security experts, who warned that they could leave the United States more vulnerable to covert influence operations. Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes compared the cuts to disabling weather monitoring during hurricane season. The entry records a reduction in staffing and coordination across agencies responsible for protecting elections. It does not claim that a specific foreign operation succeeded as a result of the changes. The central issue is whether the federal government retained enough personnel and expertise to identify and publicly counter foreign interference while securing voting infrastructure. The developments also raised questions about how the administration defined the mission and whether officials who had performed it were removed for policy or political reasons.

title: Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner Use Personal Email for Government Business
description_short: Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner Use Personal Email for Government Business
description_medium: Reports in September 2017 said Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner had used personal email accounts for some White House business. Kushner’s lawyers acknowledged the practice and said relevant messages were being forwarded to official accounts for preservation. The issue drew comparisons with Donald Trump’s campaign attacks on Hillary Clinton over private email use. The reporting raised federal records-law and transparency concerns but did not establish that every message was lost or improperly handled.
description_long:
In September 2017, reporting revealed that Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner had used personal email accounts for some White House business. Kushner’s lawyers acknowledged his use of a private account and said relevant messages were being forwarded to official government accounts. American Oversight separately reported that emails showed Ivanka had also used a personal account while serving in the White House.

The practice drew attention because Donald Trump had campaigned against Hillary Clinton’s use of a private email server, with supporters chanting “Lock Her Up.” The comparison raised questions about a double standard and about compliance with federal records requirements, including the Presidential Records Act. The available reporting described forwarding messages for preservation, so the entry should not imply that all communications were destroyed or that a court found a violation. It documents the use of personal accounts for official business by two senior presidential advisers and the resulting records-management concerns. The incident also illustrates the importance of preserving government communications regardless of which account an official uses.

title: Trump: Jared Kushner attends lunch meeting with Russian agent Dimitri Simes
description_short: Trump: Jared Kushner attends lunch meeting with Russian agent Dimitri Simes
description_medium: On March 14, 2016, Jared Kushner attended a small lunch organized by the Center for the National Interest, where former national security adviser Henry Kissinger discussed U.S.-Russia relations. The group was led by Dimitri Simes, a prominent Russia-policy commentator. The timeline later connects Simes and the center to a foreign-policy event for Donald Trump and a meeting with Russian ambassador Sergey Kislyak. The lunch itself is documented as an event, not evidence of a covert agreement.
description_long:
Jared Kushner attended a small lunch on March 14, 2016, organized by the Center for the National Interest, a Washington foreign-policy organization led by Dimitri Simes. Henry Kissinger, the center’s honorary chairman and a former national security adviser, spoke to attendees about U.S.-Russia relations. The organization had been established by former President Richard Nixon, and the Nixon family later distanced itself from Simes over his views on Russia and Vladimir Putin.

The timeline places the lunch in the context of later contacts: the Center for the National Interest hosted a foreign-policy event for Donald Trump the following month, where Trump and associates met Russian ambassador Sergey Kislyak. Kushner later discussed his relationship with Simes in a statement to Congress. Those later developments provide context but do not change what is known about the March lunch. The entry records Kushner’s attendance at a policy discussion with a prominent Russia specialist and the subject of the discussion. It does not establish that Simes was an intelligence agent or that Kushner’s participation was part of an undisclosed arrangement.

title: Trump: Giuliani leaves voicemail asking GOP to further delay Biden certification
description_short: Trump: Giuliani leaves voicemail asking GOP to further delay Biden certification
description_medium: Around 7 p.m. on January 6, 2021, Rudy Giuliani left a voicemail on Senator Mike Lee’s phone asking Senator Tommy Tuberville to delay certification of Joe Biden’s electoral victory for at least 24 hours. Giuliani said Republicans should object to more states and use the delay to obtain further information. Trump had called Lee’s phone minutes earlier looking for Tuberville. Congress was preparing to resume certification after the Capitol attack.
description_long:
Around 7 p.m. on January 6, 2021, before Congress reconvened after the Capitol attack, Rudy Giuliani left a voicemail for Senator Tommy Tuberville on Senator Mike Lee’s phone. Giuliani asked Tuberville to help delay certification of the electoral vote for at least another 24 hours. He urged Republicans to object to additional states and said the delay would give them more time to obtain information. Donald Trump had called Lee’s phone minutes earlier looking for Tuberville.

The message came as Congress prepared to resume the count that had been interrupted by the attack. Giuliani’s request was an effort to extend objections to the 2020 election results after the violence at the Capitol, rather than a routine procedural inquiry. The entry identifies the intended recipient, the device on which the voicemail was left, and the requested delay. It also notes that Giuliani contacted another senator whose identity was not publicly disclosed. The record documents the post-attack effort to keep certification stalled and its connection to Trump’s search for Tuberville. It does not imply that Tuberville agreed to Giuliani’s request or that the requested additional 24 hours was granted.

title: Trump picks soldiers based on politics, appearance to attend speech
description_short: Trump picks soldiers based on politics, appearance to attend speech
description_medium: On June 10, 2025, Trump delivered a political speech to soldiers at Fort Bragg, criticizing California Governor Gavin Newsom, Joe Biden, and the media. Military.com later reported that leaders of the 82nd Airborne Division selected audience members based on political views and appearance, including instructions not to choose “fat soldiers.” Internal messages also said soldiers opposed to the administration could ask to be replaced. The account raised concerns about partisan use of military personnel.
description_long:
Donald Trump spoke to a crowd of soldiers at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, on June 10, 2025. During the address he criticized California Governor Gavin Newsom, former president Joe Biden, and news organizations. Military.com reported that internal 82nd Airborne Division communications showed leaders had curated the audience for the event, selecting soldiers based partly on political views and physical appearance. One message said, “no fat soldiers,” while another said soldiers who opposed the administration could speak with leadership and be replaced in the audience.

The report described the effort as a staged backdrop for a political speech and noted that the visible soldiers were almost exclusively men. Military rules restrict partisan political activity by service members, and the source said it was unknown whether those involved would face discipline. The entry documents both Trump’s speech and the reported process used to select the audience. It does not establish that every soldier present shared the administration’s views or that disciplinary action followed. The episode raised questions about whether active-duty personnel were being used to create the appearance of military support for partisan remarks.

title: Trump: Young Don Jr: My dad loves his money, and that's it
description_short: Trump: Young Don Jr: My dad loves his money, and that's it
description_medium: In September 1990, Vanity Fair published an account of the strained relationship between Donald and Ivana Trump. Friends interviewed for the article recalled that 12-year-old Donald Trump Jr. had told his father he loved money more than his family. The anecdote was reported secondhand by people close to Ivana, and its exact date was unknown. The entry documents a family story printed in a magazine, not a contemporaneous recording or independently verified exchange.
description_long:
Vanity Fair’s September 1990 feature “After the Gold Rush” examined the deteriorating relationship between Donald and Ivana Trump. Friends interviewed for the article recalled an earlier conversation in which 12-year-old Donald Trump Jr. challenged his father, asking how he could claim to love his children and saying, “You just love your money.” The exact date of the exchange was not established. The account also reported that Trump’s mother, Mary, asked Ivana what kind of son she had created.

The story was based on recollections from friends of Ivana rather than a recording or direct interview with the child. The entry therefore preserves the quote as a reported family anecdote and attributes it to the magazine’s sources. It offers a glimpse of how people close to the family described the relationship at the time, but it cannot independently verify the words or the circumstances of the exchange. The record’s focus is the publication of the anecdote and the criticism it conveyed about Trump’s priorities. It should not be treated as a formal statement by Trump Jr. or as a verified transcript of a private conversation.

title: Donald Trump threatens to send police to polling places, voter intimidation
description_short: Donald Trump threatens to send police to polling places, voter intimidation
description_medium: In an August 20, 2020 Fox News interview, Donald Trump said he planned to have sheriffs, law enforcement, U.S. attorneys, and attorneys general at polling places on Election Day. Legal experts said a president could not dispatch federal officers to polling locations and that federal law restricts armed forces at polls. The comments raised concerns about voter intimidation, although the entry does not show that Trump’s proposed deployment occurred.
description_long:
During a Fox News interview with Sean Hannity on August 20, 2020, Donald Trump said he wanted sheriffs, law-enforcement officers, U.S. attorneys, and attorneys general present at polling places on Election Day. The statement prompted concern because federal law limits the presence of troops or armed federal personnel at polling sites, and legal experts said the president could not order local officers to monitor polling locations. Trump’s remarks came amid repeated claims about election fraud and a campaign focused on election security.

The entry records a public proposal and the legal objection it drew, rather than an actual deployment. A candidate’s campaign could hire off-duty officers under certain circumstances, but that is different from the government sending law enforcement to polling places. Experts warned that an official presence could intimidate voters or interfere with election administration. The account does not show that the proposed federal or local deployment took place, nor does it identify specific polling sites affected. The event matters because presidential rhetoric about law-enforcement presence can shape perceptions of whether voting is safe and free from coercion, even when the described plan is not implemented.

title: Trump admin helps Capital One cheat customers out of $2 billion
description_short: Trump admin helps Capital One cheat customers out of $2 billion
description_medium: On February 27, 2025, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, led by acting director Russell Vought, dismissed its lawsuit against Capital One with prejudice. The suit alleged that the bank misled customers about a savings account that paid substantially more interest than a similarly named account, causing an estimated $2 billion loss. The CFPB did not explain why it dropped the case. The dismissal ended the agency’s action but was not a court finding that the bank had cheated customers.
description_long:
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau under acting director Russell Vought voluntarily dismissed its lawsuit against Capital One on February 27, 2025. The agency had accused the bank of misleading customers about two similarly named savings accounts, one of which paid substantially more interest. Former CFPB director Rohit Chopra said customers had not been informed that the accounts differed and that the alleged conduct could have cost them about $2 billion.

The dismissal was with prejudice, meaning the CFPB could not revive the same lawsuit. The agency did not provide an explanation for ending the case. Because the claims were no longer litigated, no court judgment established whether Capital One violated consumer-protection law or how much customers may have lost. The entry documents a decision by the Trump administration’s CFPB to abandon a major consumer case and the questions it raised about enforcement priorities. It does not present the $2 billion allegation as an adjudicated loss or the dismissal as proof that the bank was cleared on the merits. The case’s withdrawal left the underlying allegations unresolved in court.
